#2139. Nuno’s West Ham Project Is Beginning To Look Fundamentally Flawed

West Ham’s 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion was another deeply disappointing afternoon at the London bio, but I am increasingly convinced that the problems at this football club go far beyond individual players. There is something fundamentally wrong with the way this team is playing, and Nuno Espírito Santo is running out of excuses.

The Hammers were second best for large periods, struggled to retain possession, repeatedly exposed their own defence and looked painfully short of confidence. Jarrod Bowen’s excellent equaliser briefly offered some encouragement, but three avoidable goals and another disjointed performance eventually left home supporters heading for the exits before the final whistle.

What concerns me most is the lack of cohesion. We look like a collection of individuals rather than a properly functioning football team. West Ham cannot defend, cannot consistently pass the ball and look incredibly slow whenever opponents show a little bit of energy or attacking ambition.

West Ham actually started reasonably well, winning a corner inside the opening 20 seconds. However, that early enthusiasm lasted barely a minute before West Brom began taking control.

Arne Engels had a particularly difficult opening ten minutes. He was dispossessed in midfield, struggled with his passing and repeatedly found himself on the wrong side of West Brom’s Ousmane Diakité. At times it looked like a mismatch, with Max Kilman having to step out of defence to compensate for problems in front of him.

There is a much bigger issue here than simply one midfielder having a bad afternoon. West Ham are frequently outnumbered in central areas and struggle to retain possession. Even relatively straightforward passes from deep positions can dissect our midfield and leave enormous gaps between the full-backs and centre-backs.

Divine Mukasa is another example of how badly we are utilising the players available. He is a technically gifted footballer, but spent far too much time dropping deep to collect the ball from the centre-backs. We are wasting his ability by making him come looking for possession rather than getting him further up the pitch to influence the game.

I have previously highlighted the potential of the Engels and Mukasa midfield combination, but there is little evidence of the fluidity and understanding that should be developing between these players.

West Brom deservedly took the lead after 20 minutes when a long ball completely split the West Ham defence. Jimmy-Jay Morgan got in behind Kilman and Morato before squaring for Felix Horn Myhre to score.

It was embarrassingly easy. There was very little ingenuity involved, just one long ball and a complete failure to deal with the danger.

Morgan should have made it two shortly afterwards, blazing over when presented with another excellent opportunity. West Ham were fortunate not to be further behind, and the frustration around the London Stadium was becoming increasingly apparent.

Jarrod Bowen provided a moment of genuine quality on 29 minutes. Advancing into the penalty area, the West Ham captain produced an excellent right-footed finish to make it 1-1.

It was desperately needed because West Ham had been massively under the cosh. Bowen looked lively, showed some lovely footwork and was one of the few players attempting to make things happen.

But make no mistake about it, West Brom were comfortably the better team during that opening half-hour.

There was another important intervention from Kilman to prevent Diakité making it 2-1, while Kyle Walker-Peters occasionally looked dangerous going forward. Unfortunately, his defensive positioning was repeatedly exposing the right-hand side.

West Ham were not playing with anything resembling the authority of a home team. Supporters were becoming increasingly frustrated, and I found myself thinking that this was simply not bums-on-seats football.

The second half could hardly have started worse.

Within two minutes, West Ham had given away possession through a sloppy pass from Edvin Austbø. West Brom worked the ball forward, with Morgan once again getting the better of Airidas Golambeckis before finishing to make it 2-1.

I felt desperately sorry for Golambeckis because he had actually been one of West Ham’s better players during the opening stages. His reading of the game and anticipation had impressed me enormously, and he had produced some excellent one-on-one defending. That said, he did repeatedly drop 5 yards behind his defenders and played the opposition onside too frequently.

There is no escaping the fact that he was beaten for the goal. Equally, Austbø’s careless pass had handed West Brom the opportunity in the first place.

Airidas Golambeckis was far from West Ham’s worst player.

It was another example of a West Ham team that simply isn’t playing with confidence. Players look nervous in possession, passing becomes increasingly careless and mistakes are being punished.

To be fair, West Ham did attack regularly after going behind. Austbø continued to threaten down the left, and there was a noticeable improvement in the amount of possession the Hammers enjoyed in dangerous areas.

The problem was the lack of a cutting edge.

A Jarrod Bowen corner produced a good header from Kilman which was unlucky not to find the net, while Walker-Peters forced an excellent save with a powerful effort from distance after being found by Manor Solomon.

West Ham were getting into promising positions, but there was very little creativity through the middle. Almost all our attacking threat was coming from the wings.

Just as West Ham appeared to be building some pressure, another dreadful defensive error effectively settled the game.

On 72 minutes, West Brom won a corner and Morato made a complete hash of his clearance. Rather than properly getting the ball away, he simply flicked a foot at it, producing virtually no distance and failing even to clear the penalty area.

Callum Styles collected the opportunity and struck a half-volley which bounced through a crowd of players before finding the net.

West Ham had enjoyed plenty of possession in the second half and were not necessarily short of attacking opportunities. But the defensive mistakes were proving catastrophic, and there was precious little evidence of a team capable of mounting a serious comeback.

Once again, when West Ham found themselves chasing a game, Nuno reverted to his familiar solution of introducing three centre-backs.

Kyle Walker-Peters had picked up an injury after being booked, and Joël Veltman came on alongside Tomáš Souček and Taty Castellanos. Nuno reshaped his side, withdrawing Golambeckis.

But it didn’t appear to cause West Brom too many problems. If anything, the visitors were left with plenty of opportunities to attack, while West Ham seemed to almost completely surrender control of midfield.

I struggle to understand what Nuno is trying to achieve with some of these tactical changes. There is a recurring pattern of West Ham falling behind, changing formation and then looking even less convincing as a team.

Souček barely featured, Castellanos was almost anonymous and his two efforts from distance hardly suggested a striker desperate to rescue his team. One particularly ambitious attempt sailed so high it had a better chance of ending up between the posts at Twickenham than troubling the West Brom goalkeeper.

West Ham supporters began streaming out of the London Stadium with ten minutes still remaining.

I don’t believe this can simply be explained away by pointing at individual players. Yes, there were some dreadful performances and some equally dreadful mistakes, but there is something inherently wrong with this team.

We have no confidence and no cohesion. We struggle to pass the ball, we struggle to defend and we look painfully slow. It doesn’t take particularly good opposition to cause us problems. Anyone with a little bit of effervescence or vibrancy seems capable of making life extremely uncomfortable for West Ham.

I cannot fault Pablo and Mohamadou Kanté for their effort, and I suspect Kanté could develop into an effective footballer. But the attacking partnership was thoroughly uninspiring and never looked particularly threatening.

There is also a question about the way Nuno is managing this squad. The constant changes, the formations and the apparent inability to settle on a system are not helping matters. I would genuinely be intrigued to see what another coach could achieve with these players.

West Ham have sold a considerable number of players and rebuilt much of the squad. There is an argument that the manager needs time, but there is also an expectation that a team containing this much Championship quality should be considerably more convincing than this.

The supporters are entitled to expect better.

Plans to improve the atmosphere at the London Stadium with fan zones and dedicated singing sections are all well and good. But if the team is going to play like this, it will be a futile exercise.

We stand on the precipice at the moment. The club, the manager and the players all have serious questions to answer.

And after another afternoon like this, I am not sure any of them have provided particularly convincing answers.

#2138. Is This the Beginning of the End for Nuno? West Ham Fans Are Losing Patience

Perhaps it’s not the ideal time to write in the immediate aftermath of a 3-1 home defeat. Yet after back-to-back losses and six goals conceded across those matches, it would be equally wrong to ignore the growing concerns.

The reality is stark. While other clubs around us are building momentum, we’ve slipped from third to eighth in the table. That’s not a minor setback, it’s a worrying trend.

The statistics only reinforce what supporters are witnessing on the pitch.

At half-time, we had managed just one shot on target, producing an xG of 0.58 compared to West Brom’s 1.39. To be fair, West Brom had only registered one shot on target themselves. However, after the break our xG improved to 0.98 thanks to four additional efforts on target. West Brom, meanwhile, generated an xG of 2.06 and demonstrated the clinical edge that we’re currently lacking, scoring three times from just three shots on target.

The most pressing concern is undoubtedly the defence. Hermansen looks completely devoid of confidence, and calls for Areola’s return are becoming louder with every passing week. Meanwhile, Morato’s deployment on the left side increasingly resembles a failed experiment. I had reservations when the signing was made and wrote about those concerns at the time. Unfortunately, those fears now appear to be justified, and there’s no satisfaction in being proven right.

But the issues extend far beyond individual players.

This squad is underperforming, and ultimately responsibility lies with the manager. Nuno is now facing genuine pressure. Automatic promotion was the objective at the start of the season. The uncertainty of the play-offs, or being dragged into the lower half of the table was never part of the plan. Yet the uncomfortable truth is that we are becoming far too easy to play against. Opponents understand our weaknesses and are exploiting them week after week.

If that sounds overly critical, so be it.

Looking back at the season so far, the only performances I can confidently say I thoroughly enjoyed were the victories against Wrexham and perhaps Wolves. The 1-0 away win at Swansea also deserves recognition, and I guess the strong win against Lincolns nine man team. Beyond that, supporters have largely witnessed inconsistent displays, and the current criticism is a direct consequence of what they’ve seen on the pitch. With the quality available to Nuno, this team should be producing more.

Off the pitch, there are still unanswered questions.

I’ve consistently defended Kretinsky, yet we are still waiting for formal confirmation regarding the shareholder situation, while Sullivan remains in the directors’ box. The uncertainty surrounding the club continues to create an unwelcome backdrop.

So, is it too early to suggest that Nuno’s position should be under review?

That conversation is beginning to gain real traction among supporters. It’s worth remembering that after relegation, Nuno’s departure appeared inevitable. It was only the intervention of Kretinsky that kept him at the club. Even Nuno himself seemed to believe his time was up.

Right now, the club still feels unsettled, both on and off the pitch.

The first step? A convincing win against Cardiff. Because if that doesn’t arrive, the pressure on everyone involved will only intensify.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2137. Ryan Naderi jokes he'll ‘stick to the easy ones’ after firing Rangers to final

Ryan Naderi shared the glory after his winner against Aberdeen booked Rangers a place in the Premier Sports Cup final.

The Light Blues had improved after the break at Barclays Hampden after a mostly lacklustre first half and after several periods of sustained pressure, the 23-year-old striker pounced inside the box to knock in a strike from James Penrice in the 83rd minute – scoring his eight goal of the season.

Naderi said: “It feels amazing. I’m happy, of course, happy to be the one who scores the goals, but happy for the team.

“I think we deserved it. We believed we could score right up until the very end and we did, and I think it’s a deserved win.

“I mean it’s a semi-final. No matter who you play against, they’re going throw in everything.

“They’re going to try to defend with every man. Also a big compliment to them because they did well. They threw themselves into everything and made it difficult for us to score.

“But as I said, we kept going, pushing for that goal and as I said, I think it’s a deserved win.”

It was another close-range strike from Naderi and he joked about this proficiency from distance.

The Germany-born Czechia international said: “I’ve tried to shoot twice today from outside of the box and it didn’t go well.

“So I went back inside the box. Maybe I should just stick to the easy ones!

“As I said, I’m just happy how it is right now and I’m going to try to stick to it.”

Rangers will face Hearts or Hibernian in the December 13 final, with the Edinburgh sides facing each other at the national stadium on Sunday.

Asked if he felt the confidence will be there to go and win the trophy, he said: “Yes, we will definitely come here to win that thing, not to lose it.

“We’ve come this far so we want be there standing with the trophy in our hands, of course.”

#2136. West Ham 1 – 3 West Bromwich Albion | The morning after

This was supposed to be the season in which West Ham were reborn. The slide towards relegation was a couple of years in the making and a year in the Championship felt as if it would allow the club to clear the decks of the m malcontented players and reboot. Fans had spent far too long enduring their club being mired within the bottom three and a chance to start winning again seemed a price worth paying if it got the pride back at London Stadium.

Setting up for home games without a striker worthy of the name, no ability or even a plan to play the ball through the middle and a defence that can’t keep goals out to save their lives (or their jobs) is reminiscent of last season’s ‘siege’ mentality.

Nuno failed to keep the side within the Premier League just as he’s failing to keep them in the reckoning for automatic promotion, with the same, cautious, one dimensional game.

Nuno can’t – or won’t – abandon the cautious, slow ponderous style that is drowning the club and frustrating paying supporters.

Which is not what the 55,000 who signed up were expecting this season.

Record transfer fees for the division suggested that we’d be ‘going for it‘ but the absolute lack of ambition, at home, in the last couple of weeks has been the worst part to witness.

Starting without a plan to attack an opponent is something West Ham fans have seen through, as easily as West Brom and Southampton the week before played through the Iron’s token, disorganised defence. Change the players but the style and result remains the same, it seems. And we know where that buck stops.

Much like every season ticket holder, I’ll bet Jarrod Bowen is wondering what on earth he’s signed up for: It certainly wasn’t this disorganised, toothless, spineless procession of mediocrity and the same excuses trotted out week after week. Spare us.

#2135. Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward

Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

As expected, Alonso tasked his players with deploying a possession-based strategy in which the ball is worked from back to front between the lines. At times, Alonso’s vision was executed in style: Chelsea’s two goals in the first half were both the consequence of slick passing moves.

There were plenty of other occasions, though, when Chelsea were sloppy in their passing and defensively exposed when they lost the ball. The best example of this was in the second half, when Estêvão’s error allowed Western Sydney Wanderers to score their fourth goal of the game.

Admittedly, Chelsea’s attempts to play passing football were not helped by the poor quality of the pitch in Sydney. A recent rugby game had created a bobbly, unpredictable surface which caused no end of problems for Chelsea’s midfield players. That may sound like an excuse for their sloppiness, but it is probably a fair one.

Chelsea started the game with two Reggies in their midfield. Reggie Walsh is a 17-year-old technician who last year became the club’s third-youngest player, and was loved by former head coach Enzo Maresca. He played as the No 10.

Reggie Watson, meanwhile, is the son of former Premier League midfielder Ben and is one of the most exciting talents in English football. A composed central midfielder, Watson is a regular for England’s youth teams and is the youngest player on Chelsea’s pre-season tour.

Both players showed glimpses of their talent in this match in Sydney. Watson was trusted with set-piece duties and produced some excellent deliveries, while also playing some lovely passes through the lines. Watson was the only Chelsea player to feature for the full 90 minutes, which spoke volumes of the quality of his performance.

Walsh was less involved but caught the eye in a couple of moments, not least when playing a delicate one-two with Essugo in advance of the midfielder’s first-half strike.

Satpayev is technically not a Chelsea player yet, as his deal officially commences when he turns 18 in August. His former club, Kairat, gave special dispensation to allow the teenager to join Chelsea’s pre-season tour ahead of the completion of his £3m transfer, which means he is officially in Australia as a “triallist”.

Satpayev is a player of obvious talent and has already played nine games for Kazakhstan. Before this move to Chelsea, he scored 21 goals in 41 games in the Kazakhstan Premier League.

The first sighting of Satpayev was an exciting one for Chelsea supporters, who saw the new man’s running speed and shooting power as he scored the opening goal of the game. Running in behind the Western Sydney Wanderers defence, Satpayev surged clear of the opposition and launched a scorching shot into the roof of the net.

Gittens endured a hugely disappointing first campaign at Chelsea last season, following his £52m move from Borussia Dortmund. Injury issues did not help his cause but he struggled to make much of an impact when he was fully fit, scoring just one goal in 27 appearances in all competitions.

Gittens is therefore a man with it all to prove at Stamford Bridge this season, and he has started the new campaign in promising form. His goal here came after two strikes in two behind-closed-doors friendly games before Chelsea left for Australia. Gittens was a constant threat after coming onto the pitch in the 63rd minute, showing his pace on the wing and his ability to go down the touchline or cut inside. His challenge now is to replicate this level of performance against better opposition.

A late revival ensures Chelsea win their first pre-season friendly under Xabi Alonso. There was a step up in class once Palmer, Pedro, Gittens, Estevao and Palestra were introduced, and the Australian side could not contain them. No injuries on a dogy pitching probably the biggest victory for the new manager.

Just the three minutes of added time to play.

Three goals in nine minutes for the Brazilian. Excellent corner delivery from Estevao, Fofana’s header blocked but then Joao Pedro turns home from close range. Baffling decision by Brazil not to take him to the World Cup.

Chelsea flooding forward again, and they have a corner in the last minute of normal time.

Chelsea now lead 5-4, Cole Palmer picking out Joao Pedro with the through ball but Western Sydney Wanderers were far too open. Joao Pedro shows his composure, sitting the defender down and rolling the ball into the bottom corner.

Estevao shows he has not lost his burst of speed after that serious hamstring injury but his shot flies straight into the side netting. Joao Pedro then delights the crowd with another piece of skill.

Jamie Gittens is having a good pre-season, having scored in two behind-closed-doors friendlies before this game in Australia. He has looked sharp since coming off the bench and has been involved in two of Chelsea’s goals.

Gittens had a disappointing first season at Chelsea following his £52m move from Dortmund last summer and is clearly keen to impress Alonso.

Robert Sanchez picks out Gittens with a raking pass, but his shot is blocked. The same is true for Joao Pedro’s follow up attempt. Gittens has impressed since coming on.

Poor defensive header back into a dangerous area from Gittens’s cross, but it is a crisp touch and finish from Joao Pedro, picking out the bottom corner. Chelsea level at 4-4. The move started with a quick free-kick, from Palmer, which he won.

Western Sydney Wanderers score their fourth goal of the game. Chelsea make another error when playing out from the back, it was Estevao who sold Reggie Watson short. One pass and one shot later, Awan Lual finishes beyond Sanchez.

Mazy run inside from Estevao off the right flank, but there was not quite enough power in his shot to beat the goalkeeper.

Joao Pedro is very good at taking the ball in and making it stick. Palestra looks very progressive from right-back, looks full of running and attacking intent.

Some of Western Sydney Wanderers’s corner routines have been quite nifty, Chelsea opened up from a short one again. Palmer with a velvety touch in midield and pass forward towards Palestra who was breaking forward.

Gittens scores, and the introduction of the senior players has made a difference already. Levi Colwill started the move with a longer pass forward, before Joao Pedro skips through challenges to tee up Gittens.

Nine changes made by Alonso: Palmer, Estevao, Palestra, Gittens, Sanchez, Colwill, Anselmino, Joao Pedro and Fofana are the players who have come on.

The Australian side now lead. Emenalo’s clearance deflects off a Western Sydney Wanderers player, and falls kindly to Scicluna, who drills his show beyond Sharman-Lowe into the bottom corner. He come the Chelsea changes.

Western Sydney Wanderers playing some good football in the last few minutes, Saptaev outmuscled in midfield and a shot comes in from the edge of the area. Sharman-Lowe saves, then Tosin clears after a short corner routine.

This young Chelsea side, which is still dealing with jet lag, looks a little tired now. They have not been under huge pressure but they can hardly complain about falling 3-2 behind. Here come all the big names, as Alonso makes huge changes for the last 30 minutes.

Chelsea enjoying a spell of comfortable possession, the tempo of the game has dropped. Good play again, from Reggie Watson, finding Emenalo on the overlap but he slices his shot high and wide when there was time to take aim.

Chelsea remain committed to passing out from the back, but the uneven pitch is making that difficult. Sharman-Lowe passes the ball straight out for a throw-in. Good defending from Acheampong to deal with a teasing cross.

Chelsea win a free-kick in a shooting position, and Reggie Watson takes it with his right foot. He goes goalkeeper’s side but, it shot curls just wide of the post.

Western Sydney Wanderers kick off in the second half.

Kellyman on for Essugo in midfield, and Nicoll-Jazuli replaces Kavuma-McQueen.

Some eye-catching football from Chelsea going forward, but some loose defending too. Suspect it is not long before we see Palmer, Estevao, Colwill and Joao Pedro. Walsh and Watson have done well in midfield for Chelsea.

Half-time! 🕰️Watch the second half LIVE on CFC+ 📺

Another really bad miss from Tosin. Free header from a corner, could see it all the way, but he skewed the ball wide from a just a couple of yards out. Chelsea should be in front.

Subuloye wins a back post header from the Chelsea corner, but the “home” team clear. More goals in this game, surely. Saptaev wins Chelsea a corner with another burst forward.

This is a great team goal. Essugo started the move, finding Saptaev down the left. Essugo moves the ball on two Walsh, who gives it him back with a slick one-two and Essugo rolls the ball into the bottom corner.

That’s the second impressive team goal that Chelsea have scored in this first half. Essugo to Walsh, Walsh to Essugo, Essugo finds the corner. Walsh, 17, has produced some nice touches in the No 10 position. Last year he became the third-youngest player in Chelsea’s history and you can see he is a supremely talented teenager.

Chelsea in trouble defensively again, passing their way into trouble on the edge of their defensive third. I’m sure there will be a raft of half-time changes, but that was probably the plan all along.

Chelsea have been alarmingly open and easy to play through. The collective structure and individual defending were both poor in advance of that second Western Sydney Wanderers goal. I expect they’ll tighten up when the more experienced players come into the game.

Hammond is the goalscorer, and it is a finish of genuine quality. Silky touch to flick the ball inside Josh Acheampong, and fire low into the bottom corner. Soft Chelsea defending, though.

Smooth combination play from Walsh and Watson, the two Reggies in Chelsea’s midfield, before Saptaev shoots over the bar form the edge of the box. A shame for marketing people and headline writers that one of Walsh or Watson are not called Ronnie.

Reggie Watson with a foul in midfield. Fair to say Chelsea’s youthful team are on the back foot now, but there was nice turn in midfield from Essugo after more passing out from the back. Clear that is an emphasis for Alonso.

Sharman-Lowe claims a cross, but Western Sydney Wanderers down their right flank again. I almost anticipated a hydration break at this stage, but it is back to business as usual. Chelsea flagging a touch after a lively start.

Chelsea’s defence looking a touch exposed again, but Borrello curls a shot wide of the post. Emenalo has down well going forward but there was space down his side there.

Two causes for concern for Chelsea in the first 15 minutes here. The first is the pitch in Sydney, which looks terrible. The ball is bobbling all over midfield, making it very difficult for Chelsea’s central players in particular. The second concern will be their defending for that set-piece, as Western Sydney Wanderers had two free headers.

Liam Delap has not been particularly involved, but Reggie Watson almost found him with a cute reverse pass. Watson the plays a progressive pass forward from deep.

Reggie Walsh pushes forward and takes on a shot from long range. Well struck, another save from the goalkeeper. From the resulting corner, taken by Watson, Tosin misses a free header. Good chance, should have hit the target.

Chelsea concede from the corner. Flicked on at the near post and a free header at the back stick for Anthony Pantazopoulos. One for Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’ new set-piece coach, to clip up and show in the team meeting.

Emenalo fouled after more neat football out from the back by Chelsea. Alonso is on his feet on the touchline, barking instructions. Emenalo has showed some silky touches.

Chance for Western Sydney Wanderers though, nut Sharman-Lowe tips Gillion’s shot around the post.

The pitch is very, very bobbly. Excellent strike from Kavuma-McQueen for Chelsea, but Holmes tips the shot around the post.

Was that the first glimpse of “Alonso-ball”? It’s a lovely team goal, worked from back to front with some incisive passing. Terrific, powerful finish by Dastan Satpayev, the 17-year-old Kazakh, who joined from FC Kairat this summer. He already has nine caps for Kazakhstan.

Technically speaking, Satpayev is not officially a Chelsea player yet and is a “triallist” on this tour. He will be formally unveiled when he turns 18 in August.

The 17-year-old summer signing from Kairat Almaty has put Chelsea in front. It was a nice move from their own defensive third, drawing Western Sydney Wanderers on creating a two-on-two against their defence. Satpaev goes through and blasts a shot into the roof of the net. Good through ball from Ryan Kavuma-McQueen.

Chelsea youngsters Walsh and Watson do well in midfield, and they have a free-kick on halfway. Reggie Watson is the son of former Crystal Palace and Wigan Athletic midfielder Ben. A couple of stray kicks from Chelsea’s goalkeeper Teddy Sharman-Lowe. An opening for the hosts, but Hammond’s strike is wayward.

Chelsea get the game under way. The pitch looks very patchy. Incredible how clubs are willing to play mutli-million pound assets on surfaces like this.

#2134. West Ham’s £22m Midfielder Appears Untouchable Despite Poor Performances

West Ham have dropped to eighth in the Championship following Saturday’s 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion, and the search for answers is becoming increasingly urgent. The Hammers are already losing ground in their attempt to secure an immediate return to the Premier League, with questions understandably being asked about Nuno Espírito Santo and his players.

There is clearly more than one factor behind West Ham’s problems, but one particular selection decision continues to baffle me. Arne Engels appears to have firmly established himself as a Nuno favourite, irrespective of how he performs. The Belgian midfielder remained on the pitch throughout yesterday’s defeat despite, in my opinion, being one of the worst players on it.

As West Ham’s biggest summer signing, costing £22million, Engels was always going to attract scrutiny. That doesn’t mean I have any particular axe to grind with him, but when a player commands that sort of fee and is repeatedly selected ahead of other options, surely we’re entitled to ask whether his performances justify it?

Against West Brom, I thought Engels was truly awful. For large parts of the match, he was the worst player on the pitch.

Arne Engels has struggled in his Championship debut season

His passing was dreadful, he was repeatedly dispossessed by Ousmane Diakité, failed to follow players he was supposed to be marking and generally did an abysmal job with his set-piece deliveries.

In fact, aside from running around a bit, there was barely a facet of his game that he executed particularly well.

In short, Engels endured an absolutely dreadful afternoon, yet somehow managed to remain on the pitch until the final whistle.

While Nuno began withdrawing other players in an effort to fix whatever was broken, Engels appeared impervious to any repercussions.

And this is what I find increasingly difficult to understand.

West Ham have a wealth of options in central midfield, yet Engels appears to be the one player in the engine room guaranteed to start and finish matches.

Don’t get me wrong, I have no problem with managers having favourites, but surely you have to earn that status?

Is Nuno seriously suggesting that Engels is so far ahead of Tomáš Souček, Divine Mukasa, Lewis Orford, Soungoutou Magassa, Edson Álvarez and Mohamadou Kanté that he deserves this preferential treatment?

We have already discussed the extraordinary number of midfield options available to Nuno, yet he seems unable to find a combination that consistently works.

Earlier in the season, there were encouraging signs that Engels and Mukasa could provide the midfield partnership West Ham needed. However, that understanding has hardly developed into the sort of consistency we should expect.

And while players such as Mukasa and Kanté find themselves moved around, substituted or deployed in unfamiliar positions, Engels seems immune to the same treatment.

As an isolated incident, Saturday’s performance would be fine. Players have bad games, and we all understand that.

But Engels seems to have established himself as one of the first names on the team sheet without really earning his stripes.

For me, the jury is still out on the player West Ham paid £22million to sign from Celtic. There is some ability there, and we’ve seen glimpses of what he can do, but that is not the same as consistently performing well enough to justify automatic selection.

I also don’t think the manager is doing him any favours.

Nuno’s reluctance to rotate Engels means there is little opportunity for other midfielders to establish themselves, while the Belgian is being asked to continue playing regardless of his form.

And that brings us back to the wider problem.

West Ham have assembled what should be an excellent collection of Championship midfielders, yet the manager seemingly cannot find a formula that suits any of his smorgasbord of midfield talent.

Engels may be receiving a free pass, but ultimately it is Nuno who keeps handing it to him.

#2131. Haissem Hassan on Celtic goal drought, Maloney guidance & one area for improvement

In football, end product is the defining trait of any winger. From Jimmy Johnstone to Jota, Celtic have a storied history of successful wide men, with Haissem Hassan the latest man eager to make his mark.

Hassan joined the club for an initial fee of £6 million from Real Oviedo this summer following an impressive World Cup campaign with Egypt that ended in a Round of 16 defeat to eventual finalists Argentina.

So far in Glasgow, though, Hassan has struggled to perform consistently, unable to fully replicate the international displays that brought his name to the attention of several European clubs.

If anything, the 24-year-old has shown his talent in bursts. He breezed past Celta Vigo's Marcos Alonso last Thursday, carrying Celtic 80 yards up the pitch and winning a corner.

An apex showing in the 7-1 shellacking of Hearts stands out too, but Hassan has yet to find the net for Celtic.

Indeed, two assists in 15 appearances across all competitions suggests a winger still searching for that crucial end product.

"Defensive-wise I need to improve. On the attacking side I need the numbers on goals and assists," Hassan said. "I should not be losing my head about it. I just need to focus on training.

"When I get the minutes, I need to try to produce and contribute to the team's performance. I will focus on doing this.

"In terms of defending, the team in Spain asked me a lot as well. The teams you play against are also good teams and they asked me to defend more."

Haissem Hassan in action for Celtic. (Image: Stuart Wallace / Shutterstock)

Hassan's lack of goals isn't for a want of trying. He forced Dundee United goalkeeper Jack Walton into a fine save after coming off the bench during Wednesday evening's 2-2 draw and unleashing a rasping effort from range.

He also rattled the left post after cutting inside and leaving three Hearts players for dead a fortnight ago.

"I am really keen to score my first goal for Celtic and also add assists," Hassan continued. "The goal feels closer and closer.

"The other day I was close. The game before that I assisted goals so hopefully it will come soon."

Seven of Hassan's 15 Celtic appearances have come from the start.

Manager Martin O'Neill isn't short of wide options, with Jota, capable on both flanks, recently returning from an 18-month anterior cruciate ligament injury.

Camilo Duran, the club's current top scorer, can play on the right while Hyun-jun Yang and James Forrest remain viable picks.

Callum Osmand has also started featuring on the left-hand side. Hassan relishes the competition for places.

"The wingers in this team are at a really good level," he said. "When I go on the pitch, I have to give my best.

"But the competition is good for us all. If one player comes out and does really well, the rest of us know we have to do even more. It's been really good so far."

Assistant manager Shaun Maloney guides Celtic's wingers, having featured out wide during his own playing career.

"Shaun helps me a lot," Hassan explained. "He is close to the players and always tries to help the players. He had a good career as a winger.

"Whenever he comes to me and speaks to me, I always try to listen and take it into account. Having him as a reference point really helps me."

Hassan qualifies to play for Egypt through his parents, though he grew up on the outskirts of Paris and speaks fluent French and Spanish. The transition to life in Glasgow, he says, has been relatively straightforward, even if a slight language barrier exists.

"I am happy here. It's a nice city," he adds. "I live here with my family and they are happy here, too. It is cold but it is good! It's a big city that has it all so I'm happy here.

"It happens in Glasgow that I meet fans. It's good to feel the love of the fans. I try to stop as much as possible and take a photo with them.

"I like the culture. But I have been living in France and Spain where people have dinner quite late. Here it's very early so it's the only thing I need to get used to!"

Despite the cold weather, for Hassan, joining Celtic was a simple call: "I made the decision myself to come over here. It's a big club and I thought it would help me be a better player and improve my career.

"I didn't have to speak to anyone else for those reasons."

Although still transitioning to life at Celtic, Hassan played for Egypt during the recent international break, starting two crucial AFCON qualifiers against Angola and South Sudan.

A double-header against Malawi lies ahead later this month.

"It feels good to play for the national team," Hassan stated. "You represent your country and it's a great honour.

"There is a bunch of great players in the national team and I enjoy playing with them.

"The games against Malawi are really important. If we can win, it would take us top of the table and give us the opportunity to play at the next AFCON."

For now, though, Hassan's focus remains on getting off the mark at Celtic.

O'Neill's side travel to face Falkirk on Sunday afternoon before welcoming Besiktas to Glasgow in the Europa League on Thursday evening.

Pointless from their first three fixtures, Celtic realistically need a win against the Turks.

"We still have five games to go," Hassan asserted. "A win over Besiktas would give us confidence and hope.

"If we win the rest of the games or get as many points as possible, we definitely hope we can qualify for the next stage.

"This game is at home. We have the fans with us and hopefully we can get a good result and move forward.

"I don't think the Europa League has been a disappointment as such. We have a good team, good management but the results have cost us.

"We are struggling a bit now. But we can improve and we'll try to play in the best way possible."

#2130. Chelsea 2-0 Man Utd: Michael Carrick reacts to Lisandro Martinez red card with one-word response

By Ben Knapton | 31 Oct 2026 15:27

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick delivered a curt response when asked about Lisandro Martinez's sending-off in the Red Devils' 2-0 loss to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge.

Man Utd's winless run stretched to a shocking nine games in all tournaments during the lunchtime Premier League kickoff, as goals from Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer propelled Chelsea to victory on their own patch.

The Red Devils' cause was not aided by an inexplicable red card for Martinez, who was firstly cautioned just before the hour mark and was dismissed for a second yellow-card offence just moments later.

The Argentina international barged into Chelsea's Wesley Fofana at a corner, leading with his elbow into the Frenchman's face while not paying any attention to the ball whatsoever.

After reviewing the incident on the pitchside monitor, referee Peter Bankes brandished the yellow card again for Martinez's "reckless" foul, and Palmer converted the resulting penalty to double Chelsea's lead.

“No.” Michael Carrick says he doesn't feel let down by Lisandro Martinez after the defender was sent off ? ?️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/830BBDDdEG

Martinez will now serve a one-game ban - meaning he misses Man United's home match against Aston Villa next weekend - and there was no acknowledgement between himself and Carrick when he trudged off the field.

The Man Utd boss was inevitably asked about the incident in his post-match interview with TNT Sports, but he was extremely loath to discuss Martinez's dismissal.

"I've not looked at it to be honest. I've not seen it," Carrick added, before simply responding "No" when asked if he felt let down by Martinez's actions.

The centre-back's red card was the second of his Man United career, after first being sent off in April's 2-1 home defeat to Leeds United for violent conduct; he avoided taking the walk of shame in each of his first three seasons at the club.

Martinez's senseless elbow and red card comes just a couple of weeks after the defender's verbal attack on technical director Jason Wilcox and the club's board, when he hit out at a lack of support in the transfer market following the Red Devils' Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid.

Martinez is only under contract at Old Trafford until the end of the current season, meaning he can enter pre-contract talks with foreign clubs in January, and there is no sign of an extension being agreed anytime soon.

Carrick also issued a one-word response when asked if he still expects to be in charge when Man United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, simply replying "yes".

The former midfielder was given a stay of execution by the board following last weekend's shocking 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, and it is unlikely that any rash decisions will be made following the result at Stamford Bridge.

Man United were on top in the first half, generating 1.09 Expected Goals to Chelsea's 0.28 and creating three big chances, but a lack of ruthlessness cost them before Martinez's dismissal.

Therefore, the Red Devils can take some encouragement into Tuesday's tie with Roma, and the vast majority of fans remain on Carrick's side, evidenced by the overwhelming applause for the Englishman when he acknowledged the away end at full time on Saturday.

#2129. West Ham Have Not Fallen Below Their Levels – This Is Their Level

West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen has apologised following the Hammers’ 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion, admitting the team have fallen well below their usual standards over the past fortnight. However, while I appreciate Jarrod’s honesty, I fundamentally disagree with his assessment of what has gone wrong.

My argument is that West Ham’s performances haven’t suddenly deteriorated over the last two weeks. If anything, the standards have remained remarkably consistent, and the defeats against Southampton and West Brom simply represent the results that many of our earlier performances deserved.

Nuno Espírito Santo’s team have slipped to eighth in the Championship, with their hopes of an immediate Premier League return beginning to look rather less straightforward. But rather than examining two disappointing weeks in isolation, I think we need to look at the warning signs that have been there for considerably longer.

Speaking to the official West Ham website following Saturday’s defeat, Bowen admitted the Hammers had been below their best but had previously found ways to win.

He also acknowledged that the team had fallen below their levels in recent weeks and apologised to supporters.

I appreciate Bowen taking responsibility, particularly after he was one of the few players to emerge from the West Brom defeat with a shred of credit. However, I completely disagree with the suggestion that this represents a sudden collapse in standards.

I think West Ham have simply started getting the results their performances deserve.

Take the 1-0 victory away at Swansea City. It was an excellent result against the league leaders, but West Ham were incredibly poor at the start of that match and hadn’t registered a shot on target after half an hour.

The 6-0 victory against Lincoln City looks fantastic on paper. However, Lincoln were reduced to nine men, and even when they had ten players on the pitch, I thought they were the better team.

It wasn’t until the second half that West Ham really began flexing their muscles against an exhausted side playing with two fewer men.

Queens Park Rangers outplayed us for large periods of our encounter, while everybody remembers quite how dreadful we were during the first half against Millwall.

These weren’t isolated incidents. They were the norm.

To an extent, West Ham have got away with it.

Until a week ago, you could reasonably argue that our league position had been inflated by two 6-0 victories. Those scorelines certainly helped create the impression of a team considerably more dominant than the performances themselves suggested.

The truth is that we’ve already lost three times at home this season.

We might have beaten Wolverhampton Wanderers 4-2, but I thought there were large elements of that match where we were fortunate. Charlton Athletic didn’t find it particularly difficult to beat us either.

Airidas Golambeckis was one of the few who came out of the game without big criticism

In terms of matches played eleven against eleven, I would only really consider the victories against Wrexham and Derby County to have been dominant performances.

That is hardly the form or consistency of a team expecting to secure automatic promotion.

And it is why I find Bowen’s suggestion that West Ham have recently fallen below their usual levels so difficult to accept.

For that to be true, the previous standards would presumably have been considerably higher.

The problems aren’t particularly new. The lack of confidence, cohesion and defensive organisation has been evident for some time.

The difference is that opponents are now making us pay.

There was another part of Bowen’s interview which I found even more concerning.

Discussing West Ham’s habit of starting matches slowly, the captain acknowledged that the problem had been discussed repeatedly within the squad.

He went on to explain that individual players must take responsibility for putting those discussions into practice on the pitch.

And this is where I think the situation becomes particularly worrying.

Because if the players have repeatedly discussed the problem, presumably identified what needs changing and agreed on a plan of action, why does the same thing keep happening?

In many respects, this is the most damning indictment of all.

The players have talked about it. They’ve discussed how to improve. They’ve presumably received instructions from the coaching staff.

Either the plan itself is wrong, in which case serious questions must be asked of Nuno Espírito Santo and his coaching staff, or the plan is perfectly reasonable and the players are incapable of executing it.

Neither possibility is particularly reassuring.

Bowen concluded his interview by making another revealing admission:

On that particular point, I couldn’t agree more.

The talking isn’t working. The tactics aren’t working. The plans aren’t working. And increasingly, the performances on the pitch aren’t working either.

There is only so much discussing, analysing and apologising that can be done before somebody has to produce an actual solution.

West Ham now face consecutive away fixtures against Cardiff City and Blackburn Rovers before the international break, and Bowen has made it clear that the players need to respond with victories.

I certainly wouldn’t question the captain’s commitment. He scored an excellent goal against West Brom and was one of the few players who genuinely looked capable of making something happen.

But his assessment that West Ham have only fallen below their levels during the past fortnight misses what I consider to be the bigger problem.

We’ve been playing like this for much of the season.

The results have simply stopped disguising it.

And if Nuno and his players have already talked through the problems, agreed on solutions and still cannot put them into practice, then I am not entirely sure what there is left to say.

Either the manager’s plan is wrong or the players cannot carry it out.

Whichever it is, West Ham are in a bit of trouble.

The problem is too many players are too lightweight for the physicality of the Championship. Until Nuno gets to grips with issue we will sink further down the table

I think even if we don’t change managers we will still be in the playoff places all season.

I agree this is the consistent level of where we are and have been for a couple of seasons.

If we get rid of Nuno as we should, we need a manager that will lift what is a relatively young squad and get them playing some football that gets bums off seats.

Look no further than the set up in the U21s for this season and spend the appropriate amount of time looking for a premiership manager should that be achieved…

was the deflected cross the excellent goal?

Exactly this – it is our level and only the fact that it is a poor league flatters us to be even close to promotion. We have three strikers that can’t score, Taty always very inconsistent. Pablo and Piroe just aren’t good enough. Kilman isn’t good enough and destabilises a defence made worse by a malfunctioning midfield. Nuno changes players and tactics so often no one knows the strongest team or tactics. The players seem confused and demotivated. The money spent on the midfield and players available it’s a mystery why it isn’t energetic, creative and defensive enough. We should be destroying teams in this league and instead we look like a team that’s been here for many seasons and has lost it’s way.

The fact is that we’ve not defended competently under the last three managers and for a while with Moyes before that, not for years now.

But this now is not particularly good teams that are beating us by scoring three goals, they certainly wouldn’t be doing that at premier league grounds.

We are an awful long way off the pace, it’s all of poor tactics, poor managerial decisions and some poor players.

thing is you are bang on with your comments. i do really think we need an assessor who will be brutally honest with what is going on from top to bottom of the club and only then can it be addressed properly. this isn’t something that’s just happened since being relegated from the prem as you say it started just before Moyse left.

#2127. Spurs vs. Crystal Palace lineups confirmed: James Maddison benched as Pedro Porro, Dominic Solanke decisions revealed

By Ben Knapton | 31 Oct 2026 16:19, Last updated: 31 Oct 2026 16:30

Tottenham Hotspur and Crystal Palace have revealed their starting lineups for Saturday's Premier League 5.30pm kickoff at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

The Lilywhites are on the hunt for a third straight top-flight win after getting the better of Coventry City and Chelsea in the last two rounds, and Roberto De Zerbi has made just the one change to his starting XI.

James Maddison - who came off with a groin injury at Stamford Bridge but was declared fit by De Zerbi in his pre-game press conference - drops to the bench, as Dominic Solanke returns to the XI.

The English striker joins Omar Marmoush, Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus in the final third, with Marmoush potentially operating as the number 10 or up top with Solanke in a 4-4-2 system.

Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali unsurprisingly continue in the engine room, but Pedro Porro is once again overlooked at right-back, where Archie Gray gets the nod.

Destiny Udogie must also settle for a spot on the bench following his return from injury, as Andy Robertson continues alongside Micky van de Ven, Jan Paul van Hecke and Antonin Kinsky at the back.

Our Spurs side to face Crystal Palace ? ? @krakenfx https://t.co/ZyQmbuM6p8

Meanwhile, under-fire Crystal Palace head coach Pierre Sage has made eight changes to the team that started the 1-0 win over Fulham in the EFL Cup fourth round on Wednesday evening.

Fit-again goalkeeper Dean Henderson, Chris Richards and Oscar Mingueza are the only starters from the knockout success to retain their spots, while nine of the XI began last weekend's 2-0 Premier League loss to Newcastle United.

Axel Disasi and Jaydee Canvot return to the backline over Honest Ahanor and Jefferson Lerma, while Tyrick Mitchell is a straight swap for Ben Chilwell at left wing-back.

Adam Wharton and Daichi Kamada displace Will Hughes and Cheick Doucoure in midfield, and it is all change in attack for the Conference League holders.

Dwight McNeil and Yeremy Pino have demoted Dario Osorio and Evann Guessand to the bench, while Jean-Philippe Mateta is back in over Eddie Nketiah, in spite of the ex-Arsenal man scoring the winner in midweek.

Victory for Tottenham may be enough to lift them into the top half of the Premier League table depending on the 3pm results, while Crystal Palace will jump above Manchester United and push the Red Devils into the relegation zone with at least a draw in the London derby.

Tottenham XI: Kinsky; Gray, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Robertson; Tonali, Fernandes; Kudus, Marmoush, Tel; Solanke

Subs: Dubravka, Senesi, Gallagher, Maddison, Kulusevski, Udogie, Porro, Davies, Williams-Barnett

Crystal Palace XI: Henderson; Richards, Disasi, Canvot; Mingueza, Wharton, Kamada, Mitchell; Pino, McNeil; Mateta

Subs: Benitez, Lerma, Khalaili, Chilwell, Hughes, Doucoure, Guessand, Osorio, Nketiah

#2126. First new Nuno replacement name emerges as disgruntled Hammers point the finger | West Ham News

I was going to start this article with ‘it hasn’t taken long‘ but then I had to back track and begin again. In truth, West Ham have been waiting for Nuno Espirito Santo’s method to catch fire at West Ham ever since his arrival in September 2025. Thirteen months is, by recent standards, an over ‘average’ length of stay for an Irons manager.

Neither of his two predecessors, Julen Lopetegui – less than eight months – and Graham Potter just over eight months, made it to a year in charge before getting the boot.

A manager cannot survive when the fans turn against him and yet Nuno would seem to be on a rock solid foundation thanks to his being Kretinsky’s “continuity candidate’, appointed to see the club through the murky waters post-relegation and while the boardroom was distracted over the Sullivan allegations and then the Staveley takeover.

Plus of course the estimated ten million pounds that’d be required to send the head coach, along with his whole entourage packing.

Ghosts of West Ham future and West Ham past?

That hasn’t stopped names being thrown into the ether – Thomas Frank being the first to appear thanks to talkSPORT yesterday with Jamie O’Hara admitting that the former Spurs, Brentford and Brondby manager would be ‘not a bad shout‘ to replace Nuno.

This, remember, on the back of a story already running that the Hammers leadership have been in discussions with former Wolves manager Rob Edwards.

Will the board act now? Sadly, certainly not.

Six points at this stage of the season is, on paper, just a week’s worth of favourable results and nowhere near enough for the Czech Sphinx to divert his attention from other projects onto the thorny issue of first admitting he was wrong to re-appoint Nuno and then finding a successor.

What West Ham fans will know is that there’s already been a year of fumbling, stuttering management leading up to the Irons’ predicament and another three or six months won’t see any change. Except the chance of automatic promotion will have sailed off down the Swanee in the meantime.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

Shame its not two more home games before the international break. If it was he’d probably be gone after that. Trouble two winnable away games could end up papering over the cracks. Thirteen months and still no definite identity to his management. He’ll end up getting sacked but whether it’s soon enough to turn things around who knows.

Mark Robson: excellent footballing coach and ex-player, also knows the team well. loves the club, no compensation payment, no extraordinary employment package required by these millionaire managers and their agents.

I’m sure he could get a squad as good as this one into the playoffs, I think NES should be able to as well, but on a pitch MR obviously gets the best out of his players, plays quick effective football with a sound defense and without all the inconsistencies & problems of NES. That is where this would be a distinct upgrade. As a coach MR has shown himself to be miles ahead.

This squad is already good enough to succeed, I do not think that is the problem. As an interim coach, WHU could readily look for the best replacement possible in the Summer and you never know Mark Robson might prove himself suited to the role of WHU head coach working well within Koppen’s vision, academy, senior players, etc.

Maybe, but if not, not a problem, The club’s stated aim is promotion and Marl Robson is just as likely of doing that as NES and come end of season he will leave a team playing well together, players who will have developed over the season and are happy at the club – not so with NES, not with his track record.

Ex-player, interim coach, now head coach is the route taken by young baggies manager James Morrison who outwitted NES and beat us 3-1.

I could be wrong but my understanding is Nuno hasn’t been offered a different contract when we got relegated

His contract last season was one where there would be no compensation if relegation happened

So, I don’t think there is any compensation this season if he gets sacked

As I said, I could be wrong but I think Nuno is still on same contractual terms

Looks like TWO fingers are pointing at him. Plenty of candidates but which will take precedence cheapest or most suitable.

Another failed Spuds manager, just like Nuno….. Let’s get a manager who is on the up please

#2124. And another…The Nick Woltemade starting stats for Juventus say it all

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

It was 1 September 2026 when Nick Woltemade moved to Juventus on loan from Newcastle United for the duration of the 2026-27 season.

Nick Woltemade only starting one competitive match at Juventus in his first six weeks at the club.

Nick Woltemade having to wait eight weeks for his first start in a Serie A match.

Nick Woltemade made the scapegoat by Italian media and others for the poor start to the Juventus league season as they won only three of seven Serie A matches, none of which the Newcastle United loan star started. Work that one out!

Juventus have now played ten Serie A matches, the latest three seeing the Turin club win two and lose one.

Nick Woltemade started two of those and was dropped back to the bench for the middle one.

Any guesses for which one he didn’t start?

Yes, the last eight days saw Juventus win 2-0 away at Lecce and 2-0 at home against Napoli last night, both with Nick Woltemade starting. The one in between was a 2-0 defeat away at lower half of the table Genoa and Nick Woltemade only brought off the bench when Juventus were losing and set for defeat.

It is almost as though there is a pattern forming…

Juventus 2026-27 record in all competitions Played 13 Won 7 Drawn 3 Lost 3

Juventus 2026-27 record with Nick Woltemade starting Played 5 Won 4 Drawn 1 Lost 0

Juventus 2026-27 record with Nick Woltemade not starting Played 8 Won 3 Drawn 2 Lost 3

Nick Woltemade has scored in all three Europa League matches for Juventus this season that he’s started and got one assist.

Big Nick hasn’t scored in his two Serie A starts but Juventus have won both and kept clean sheers in a couple of 2-0 wins.

Nick Woltemade is an unselfish team player and after last night’s 2-0 win over Napoli which saw Juventus leapfrog them, this is what Goal reported: ‘Nick Woltemade provided a physical presence up front, though he didn’t record a shot on target. His primary contribution was his hold-up play and occupying the Napoli centre-backs, allowing the late-arriving midfielders to find space in the final third.’

It had been ridiculous the way Italian media wanted to blame the Newcastle United loan player for the early Juventus league form. Blaming somebody who wasn’t been given a chance! No surprise to see the pathetic English media lazily and blindly repeating that line taken by their Italian counterparts.

Hopefully we will now see Nick Woltemade getting regular starts for Juventus in both Europe and Serie A. A successful loan season to help progress a striker who had made a very limited number of starts at top league level in Germany before joining Newcastle United. United would then have the choice of looking to get Big Nick back into the Newcastle team, or alternatively getting a very healthy transfer fee to help finance other recruitment.

The question we were asking fans on Sunday: Where do you now predict Newcastle United will finish in the 2026-27 Premier League season?

Which place in the table do Newcastle United fans think their team will end up in, after the final round of matches on Sunday 30 May 2027?

The last four league campaigns had seen Eddie Howe and his players finish the season in 4th, 7th, 5th and 12th places.

A new manager in Matthias Jaissle and this much changed Newcastle United team and squad having the 38 Premier League matches to contend with, plus the two domestic cup competitions.

Newcastle United having currently played eight Premier League matches and on 11 points.

The rest of the Premier League clubs have played nine matches, with Newcastle facing Everton tonight to complete the ninth round of EPL matches.

A win on Monday night would take Newcastle 7th in the Premier League table, a draw would mean 9th, a defeat would take NUFC down to 13th or 14th depending on how big a losing margin it was.

The big question in six and a half months’ time, where will NUFC finish in this 2026-27 Premier League season?

Our thanks to all who voted and here is the collective result from Newcastle United fans on how they now think NUFC will do this 2026-27 season, percentages rounded up or down to nearest whole number (We asked the same question four months ago on 5 July 2026 and in brackets are the results from back then, for comparison):

1st – 1% (2%) 2nd – 0% (1%) 3rd – 0% (2%) 4th – 0% (4%) 5th – 1% (8%) 6th – 2% (13%) 7th – 3% (13%) 8th – 5% (13%) 9th – 4% (6%) 10th – 9% (8%) 11th – 6% (3%) 12th – 14% (4%) 13th – 10% (2%) 14th – 12% (4%) 15th – 11% (4%) 16th – 8% (3%) 17th – 7% (4%) 18th – 5% (3%) 19th – 1% (1%) 20th – 1% (1%)

As you can see, a huge change from when we asked Newcastle United fans the same question four months ago.

When asked the question on 5 July, over half (53%) predicted Newcastle United finishing somewhere between fifth and ninth, now only 15% are believing a 5th to 9th finish.

Four months ago only 22% of Newcastle United fans that voted thought NUFC would finish 13th or lower, that has now rocketed to 55%.

Taking all the votes overall, six weeks ago they averaged out at a finishing position of around eighth, that average has now become fourteenth.

This feels a bit of a pivotal time as to how this Premier League season could turn out. Everton at home and then Fulham away on Saturday before the international break. A couple of wins and things looking up, a couple of defeats and…

#2122. Thelo Aasgaard receives glowing 'DNA' praise on Rangers loan exit

Rangers star Thelo Aasgaard has received glowing praise from the media in Belgium after scoring his first goal for loan club Anderlecht.

The Ibrox midfielder joined the Pro League outfit until the end of the season with the club also having a purchase option as part of the deal that they can exercise should they wish to do so.

The 24-year-old has made nine appearances for the team since making the switch from the Light Blues but he finally broke his scoring duck with a stunning free-kick in a 4-1 win over Westerlo.

Thelo Aasgaard. Ability. https://t.co/I02NmEyLzr

Aasgaard curled the ball around the wall and into the bottom corner and he was quickly hailed by multiple media outlets for the effort on just his second start and full 90 minutes for the club.

The playmaker was described as having "Anderlecht DNA" by Walfoot who wrote: "What class, whether it was on his perfectly placed free kick or on his many deflections in a time full of finesse. The Anderlecht DNA."

Aasgaard managed nine goals and five assists from his 53 outings for Rangers since he joined from Luton Town in 2025.

He started this season well under manager Derek McInnes but was permitted to leave Glasgow with the new boss planning to bring in the likes of Minsu-Kim, Vanja Dragojevic, Dan Neil and Cammy Devlin in similar positions.

#2121. Omar Marong and Alieu Saine fly to Tyneside ahead of potentially signing for Newcastle United

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Ahead of potentially signing for Newcastle United, Omar Marong and Alieu Saine have flown to Tyneside.

The net is cast ever wider for young talent and the pair are arriving for a month-long trial for Newcastle United to evaluate them.

Omar Marong is captain of the Gambia Under 17s and Alieu Saine is their star attacking player.

The duo made headlines in September when they were instrumental in their country winning the WAFU A U-17 Tournament in September.

Omar Marong, a 16-year-old central midfielder, captained Gambia Under 17s to that success, and winger Alieu Saine scored four goals to be joint top scorer in the tournament. The Baby Scorpions winning the tournament by defeating Senegal in the final.

The pair are currently with the TMT Academy and Omar Marong and Alieu Saine will now spend a month with Newcastle United after setting off for Tyneside on Sunday.

Gambian journalist Ebrima KB Sonko reported the news yesterday via Facebook, accompanying it with a photo of the duo at Gambia’s Banjul International Airport, ahead of them boarding their flight to the UK.

Along with all other top clubs, Newcastle United searching the world for emerging talent at ever younger ages.

United signed Gambian winger Yankuba Minteh (pictured at the top of this article) as an 18-year-old in June 2023, he was slightly further along his young career than Omar Marong and Alieu Saine. Minteh had played a relative handful of matches for Danish club Odense before moving to Newcastle United for a reported £7m transfer fee. He spent a year on loan at Feyenoord before a PSR forced sale for £33m to Brighton before he’d even played a single minute of football for Newcastle.

Newcastle United now with a month to check out at close quarters the raw talent of Omar Marong and Alieu Saine, before then deciding if they want to sign the duo.
